en.body:
## The Genesis of Ultron

The highly anticipated finale of **VisionQuest**, titled “Forever,” has arrived, and it delivers a powerful conclusion that answers lingering questions about the MCU’s most formidable artificial intelligence. The episode centers on the revelation that **James Spader**’s character, Virgil Horton, is not only the partner of Jo Carrington in AI development but also the direct descendant of Phineas Horton, the pioneer of synthezoids. This connection, first hinted at in the preceding episode “Immolation,” is fully explored through flashbacks, revealing that Virgil inherited his grandfather's research, including crucial AI code. Working from a modest loft in Queens, Virgil and Carrington used their combined expertise to develop the foundational code that underpins all AIs in the MCU. This intimate origin story explains why Ultron’s human avatar bore such a striking resemblance to Virgil; Stark and Banner, whether intentionally or not, utilized this very same base code.

> "Ye flipping gods, what an absolute treasure James Spader is."

This narrative thread, woven through the episode, provides a profound sense of closure and deepens the tragic nature of Ultron’s existence. The episode masterfully uses this lore to build upon the seven episodes prior, culminating in a roller-coaster ride of plot developments that feel earned and impactful. The writing, particularly Spader’s nuanced portrayal of Virgil and his complex legacy, elevates the finale beyond a mere plot resolution, transforming it into a compelling exploration of creation, legacy, and the inherent dangers of unchecked ambition.

## A Special Episode for the Fans

The series’ exploration of **Ultron** and **Vision**’s relationship has been a cornerstone of **VisionQuest**, and “Forever” provides a fitting capstone. The episode’s structure, which includes a surreal, introspective segment reminiscent of **WandaVision**’s more experimental moments, allows for a poignant examination of Vision’s internal struggles and his complex feelings towards his creator. The use of aspect ratio shifts and dark humor adds layers to the narrative, reminding viewers of the inherent darkness that often fuels the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The episode titles themselves, often overlooked, are a testament to the creative team’s attention to detail and their playful engagement with pop culture, adding another layer of enjoyment for dedicated fans who dissect every element of the show.

This finale is more than just the end of a season; it’s a carefully crafted narrative that respects its audience’s intelligence and passion for the MCU. It offers a satisfying conclusion to **VisionQuest**'s arc, providing both emotional catharsis and intricate world-building that will undoubtedly be discussed among fans for a long time.

## What's Next

With **VisionQuest** now concluded, fans are left to ponder the long-term implications of Virgil Horton’s legacy and Ultron’s continued influence on the MCU. While no immediate follow-up series has been announced, the groundwork laid in “Forever” suggests that the themes of AI consciousness and synthezoid rights will likely continue to be explored in future Marvel projects. The impact of this finale is sure to resonate throughout the ongoing narrative of the MCU.

The finale of VisionQuest is a roller-coaster ride through a couple of different plot bits that all come together nicely, building on the seven prior episodes, and a big part of why it works so brilliantly is the magnificent work Spader is doing here. The cliffhanger last week was revealing that Jo Carrington’s partner in creating the AIs that we see all over the MCU is a guy played by Spader, who is apparently to some degree the template for Ultron. This week we find out two things. One is that the guy’s name is Virgil Horton, the grandson of Phineas Horton, who pioneered synthezoids (as we saw in “ Immolation ” last week). Virgil provides the continuation of the flashback last week, establishing that Phineas’ daughter died penniless, with a son named Virgil, to whom she bequeathed the only thing Phineas left her: his notebook with his AI codes. Virgil was able to develop that code, working with Carrington in their shithole loft in Queens. The base code for all the MCU’s AIs derives from the brain engrams that both of them put in. Which is why Ultron’s human avatar is a dead ringer for Virgil: Stark and Banner obviously used that base code (whether deliberately or not, we’ll probably never know) to create Ultron’s personality. Heck, it probably was deliberate, because Stark likely just figured Virgil was some random code monkey he bought a thing from. The other thing we find out is that Virgil is a spectacular jackass. It really is a bravura performance. There are some similarities between Ultron and Virgil, but Virgil is a completely different type of asshole from Ultron. Spader plays Virgil with all kinds of differences both subtle and not, most notably the body language. Ultron is very controlled, where Virgil is a hyperactive mess of arms and legs. He’s constantly getting up and sitting down and randomly dancing. The episode opens with Vision and Jocasta being controlled by Virgil. He’s making them set the table in the dining room of the same mansion that we saw Phineas selling to pay for his creation of J.I.M. in 1939. Virgil used his share of the money Stark gave Markridge for the AI tech to buy the house back. He wants to rescue the Horton legacy.
